4

  • T: of Ḫuwawa, whom your mind does ever fear.
  • L: huwāwa ← Humbaba I; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ittanandaru ← adāru II “to be afraid (of), fear”; kabtatka ← kabattu I “liver, also innards”

5

  • N: attā | tattakkip-ma || kīma lēʾim | tušabraqšu
  • T: You will lock horns and batter him like a bull,
  • L: attā ← attā I “you (2 m. sg. pron.)”; tattakkip-ma ← nakāpu I “to push, thrust Bab., NA”; kīma ← kīma I “like”; lēʾim ← lī'u I “bull O/jB offered, slain, eaten”; tušabraqšu ← barāqu I “to lighten, shine Bab.(lit.)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 244]: “The line divides into two equal halves, with a pause at the caesura: átta | tattakkípma || kīma lé’im | tušabráqšu. The bull belongs with the second verb. Renger read tušaprakšu and translated ‘als war er ein Ringer, wirst [Du] ihm (den Hals) zur Seite drehen’; this is perhaps reading too much into šupruku, ‘to put in the way’. Hecker follows Renger but I side with Bottéro, Tournay and Shaffer, who render the clause ‘tu l’abattras comme un taureau’. The bull develops the imagery of the first part of the line in a way that a wrestler would not. The causative stem of barāqu is used figuratively for violent destruction of an enemy: see the passages quoted in CAD B, p. 104, 2 c, and note Malku I 107: šub-ru-qu = da-a-ku, ‘to kill’ ([temp_id_2401129561684543: 426]).”
NipOB1 o 5-6. at-ta ta-at-ta-ak-ki-ip-ma ki-ma le-i-im | ($___$) tu-ša-ab-ra-aq-šu

6

  • N: rēšīšu | tušappal | ina dannūtīka
  • T: you will force his head down with your strength.
  • L: rēšīšu ← rēšu I “head”; tušappal ← šapālu I “to be(come) deep, low”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; dannūtīka ← dannūtu I “strength, power Ass., O/jB”
  • Note: See [RN117: 244]: “The significance of forcing the bull’s head down (flat on the ground?) is probably that this is how a bull-wrestler breaks a bull’s neck. Contra Hecker, TUAT III/4, p. 661, fn. 6a, rēšīšu is not plural but dual, as often.”
NipOB1 o 7. re-ši#-šu tu-ša-ap-pa-al i-na da-an-nu-ti-ka

7

  • N: puršumum | ša tāmuru || ilka | wīru(m)
  • T: The old man you saw is your mighty god,
  • L: puršumum ← puršumu I “old (man) O/jB, NA”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; tāmuru ← amāru I “to see”; ilka ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; wīru(m) ← īru I “~ strong jB lex.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 244–245]: “Others have taken wi-ru as the god Wēr, though Renger and Bottéro drew attention to the problem such an interpretation posed with regard to the Yale tablet, where Wēr is the guardian of the Cedar Forest and thus an ally of Gilgameš’s enemy (OB III 131). Here, as elsewhere in the epic, Gilgameš’s god is not Wēr but Lugalbanda (see OB III 271, OB Harmal 15–16 and SB VI 165), and Wēr is thus quite out of place for this reason too. Accordingly one is led to look for a suitable adjective or common noun that can be written wi-ru. The existence of such a word can perhaps be supported by the lexical entry Malku I 52: i-ru = ga-aš-ru ([temp_id_2401129561684543: 425; also p. 435], Explicit Malku I 143). This adjective probably also appears in the OB text about Narām-Sîn and Erra, where Erra is described as wi-ru-um ša-ka-al-mu-šu, ‘mighty terror’ ([RN2008a: 361, 37; cf. note on p. 363]). The absence of mimation in our text is unusual, but note also da-an-nu in rev. 6'.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "Schøyen₃" b+7'
NipOB1 o 8. pu-ur-šu-mu-um ša ta-mu-ru-u₂ il-ka we-ru

  • T: the one who begot you, Lugalbanda.’
  • L: bāni ← banû IV “to create”; qaqqadīka ← qaqqadu I “pl. f. head”; lugalbanda ← Lugalbanda I
  • Note: See [RN117: 245]: “As W. G. Lambert tells me (private communication), the phrase bāni qaqqadim in the meaning ‘father, sire’ is a calque from Sumerian sag.du₃ (var. du/dug₄), for which see G. R. Castellino, Two Šulgi Hymns (BC), p. 181; Å. W. Sjöberg, TCS III, p. 54. Note especially in an inscription of Samsuiluna: {dnanna dingir sag.du.mu.še₃} : a-na {dEN:[ZU] DINGIR ba-ni-ia}, ‘for Sîn, the god who begot me’ (D. Frayne, RIME 4, p. 381, 41–2 // 39).”
NipOB1 o 9. ba-ni# qa₂-qa₂-di-ka {d}lugal-ban₃-da

10

  • N: etqet | eli šalaštin | šunātīya
  • T: it surpasses my (other) three dreams!
  • L: etqet ← etēqu I “to go past”; eli ← eli I “on, over, above”; šalaštin ← šalāš I “st. abs.”; šunātīya ← šuttu I “pl. šunātu(m) dream š. naṭālu, amāru etc. to have a dream, to…”
  • Note: See [RN117: 245–246]: “For a plene spelling comparable to e-et-qe₃-et, and from the same verb, see the imperative e-et-qa₂-ni-i-ma, ‘pass me by!’, in the OB narrative poem about Narām-Sîn and Apišal (v 7; [RN262: 182]). The form šalaštin compares, as Renger noted, with erbettin in ki-ib-ra-a-at er-be₂-ti-in, ‘four world-regions’, in a fragmentary OB text about Sargon of Akkade (BRM IV 4, 4–5, ed. [RN262: 34]). The parallel is more instructive than Renger saw, however, for the gender of the number is the same as the noun. The absence of polarity thus marks the phrase šalaštin šunātīya as comprising two nouns, though in apposition rather than in a possessive construction such as kibrāt/sūq/šār erbettim. Usual language would yield šalāš šunātīya. šalaštum is a group of three (‘triad’) comparable with erbettum, ‘group of four’, ḫamiltu, ‘group of five’, and sebettum, ‘heptad’. For nunation in OB see now GAG³ §§44c (possessive pronouns), 63c (miscellaneous).”
NipOB1 o 11. e-et-qe₃-et e-li ša-la-aš-ti-in šu-na-ti-ia#

  • N: appalsam-ma | anzâm | ina šamê
  • T: I watched an Anzû-bird in the sky,
  • L: appalsam-ma ← palāsu I “to look (at)”; anzâm ← Anzû I “Anzû”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; šamê ← šamû I “mostly pl. tant. sky, heaven”
NipOB1 o 12. ap#-pa-al-sa₃-am-ma {d}IM.DUGUD{mušen}-am i-na ša-ma-i

12

  • N: itbē-ma | kīma erpeti || išaʾʾu | elni
  • T: up it rose like a cloud, soaring above us.
  • L: itbē-ma ← tebû I “OAkk, Ass. tabā'u(m), NB tabû to get up, arise, set out”; kīma ← kīma I “like”; erpeti ← erpetu I “cloud Bab. red, black etc.”; išaʾʾu ← šâ'u I “to fly O/jB”; elni ← eli I “on, over, above”
  • Note: See [RN117: 245–246]: “At the beginning of the line the reading itbēma (against Renger: š[a] x x), which Bottéro (‘il s’élança’, also Tournay and Shaffer) and Hecker (‘er erhob sich’) also saw, means that i-ša-ú is not the present subjunctive of the ‘hollow’ root √šūʾ, but the plain present of a variant II+III-Aleph root (u/u). As Renger noted, šâ’u also describes the characteristic behaviour of the mythical lion-headed eagle, the Anzû-bird, in an inscription of Aššurnaṣirpal II (now Grayson, RIMA 2, p. 260, 74). The verb seems to cover soaring, wheeling and swooping, that is, the flight pattern typical of large birds of prey. Division of the poetic line into units indicates that the simile occurs before the caesura and so belongs in the first clause not the second: itbēma | kīma érpetim || išáʾʾu | elīni.
NipOB1 o 13. it#-be₂#-ma ki#-ma er-pe-tim i-ša-u₂ el-ni

13

  • N: ... | šunnû | pānūša
  • T: It was a …, its face was very strange,
  • L: šunnû ← šanû IV “to be changed, become different”; pānūša ← pānu I “front, pl. face”
  • Note: See [RN117: 246]: “To my eyes the traces of the first word do not allow Renger’s nap-lu-uh₂-tum-ma, ‘da war eine Schreckensgestalt’, though it cannot be discounted that some of the traces on my copy are remnants of poorly erased signs. I can offer no firm decipherment, only the comment that du!-lu!-uh₂-tum-ma, ‘there was confusion’, is as likely as napluḫtumma, if not more so. One must also bear in mind that in the parallel line, rev. 2', the space suggests that <the> word is written more concisely, with three signs instead of four. The word šunnû could also be translated ‘double’, but here probably has implications of monstrousness (cf. Bottéro, ‘son aspect était monstreux’). The face of Anzû, the lion-headed eagle, was a by-word for horror, even the very image of death, as we know from Enkidu’s dream on his death-bed (MB Ur 65–6 // SB VII 168–9) and elsewhere (see the commentary on MB Ur 66).”
  • Parallels: L I.4 OB "Nippur" a+2
NipOB1 o 14. x x-uh₂-tum-ma šu-un-nu-u₂ pa-nu-u₂-ša

a+4

  • N: šalummassa | tapallaham | attā
  • T: While you fear its awesome splendour,
  • L: šalummassa ← šalummatu I “~ radiance Bab., Bogh., Ug. of deities, king, temple, cult…”; tapallaham ← palāhu I “to fear, revere”; attā ← attā I “you (2 m. sg. pron.)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 246 ad 4′–5′]: “The structure of the couplet is enhanced by the opposition of atta and anāku. The first word of l. 5' remains a problem. Renger proposed derivation from etēmum, and translated ‘werde ich anstoßen’, but the meaning of this verb is very obscure. A more secure candidate is ṭênum (e-ṭe₄-en, ‘I shall mill’), but the sense leaves a lot to be desired. The unusual spelling of ušetbēka recalls the use of CV signs for VC in an older tradition of orthography, as for example at Ebla. On this see below, the introduction to OB Harmal₂.”
